hands of a keyholder, whose names are on the list by the safe. The first-aid kit is checked monthly

provenance.key: Volunteer Notes for the Harbourside Lifeboat Museum

The Harbourside Lifeboat Museum occupies the old boathouse at the end of the east pier and is run
entirely by volunteers. These notes are for anyone taking a shift on the door, in the boat hall or in
the workshop, and they assume no knowledge of boats, of museums or of the sea. Everything a
volunteer needs in order to open the building, look after its visitors and close it again is written
here, and where it is not, the person to ask is named.

The museum exists because the station moved to the new slipway in 1994 and the town declined to
let the boathouse be sold. The building had housed a lifeboat since 1867, and the crew lists on the
wall inside the door run without a gap from that year to the last launch. A trust was formed, the
council granted a lease, and the first volunteers opened the doors the following summer with a
single boat, a borrowed till and a hand-lettered sign. Most of what is described in these notes grew
out of that first season.

There are three boats on display and one in the workshop. The oldest is a pulling and sailing boat of
1902, restored over eleven winters; the largest is the motor lifeboat that served here from 1951 to
1978; the smallest is an inshore inflatable that most visitors recognise at once. The boat in the
workshop is a private restoration on loan, and the owner works on it on Thursdays. Visitors may
watch from the rail but may not enter the workshop, however friendly the invitation sounds.

Opening up takes two people and about twenty minutes. One unlocks the side door, disarms the
alarm within the sixty seconds it allows, and switches on the hall lights from the panel by the stairs.
The other walks the boat hall with the checklist, looking for anything that has moved, dripped or
been left behind, and initials the sheet on the office door. The front doors are opened last, at ten
exactly, because there is nearly always somebody waiting and it is better that they see a building
that is ready for them.

The till is counted at opening and at closing and the float is kept at forty pounds in coin. Card
payments go through the reader on the counter, which needs the office wifi and occasionally needs
the office wifi turned off and on again. Takings are bagged, labelled with the date and both
volunteers' initials, and locked in the safe; nobody carries cash home. The bank run is done on
Mondays by whichever trustee is on the rota, and the rota is pinned on the office wall beside the
safe.

Admission is free and donations are invited, which means the collecting box by the door matters
more than the shop. It is emptied weekly, counted by two people, and the total is written on the
whiteboard in the office where every volunteer can see it. A month in which the box does badly is
usually a month in which the door has not been staffed, and the whiteboard is there so that the
connection is visible to everyone rather than only to the treasurer at the year end.
